c.tagline: France in the Amazon – Creole markets, colonial squares, and a rocket base next door.

taxi.fareNote: No Uber or ride-hail apps operate here; taxis are booked by phone or found at stands – metered but with higher night, Sunday and holiday rates, so agree the fare for airport runs.

emergency.note: 112 is the general EU emergency number; 15 reaches the SAMU medical service and 17 the police.

avoid.reason: Avoid the Village Chinois quarter (nicknamed 'Chicago') near the canal, notorious for drug-related crime, especially after dark.
Muggings occur after dark even near Place des Palmistes — take taxis at night and keep phones out of sight.

hood_desc: The old colonial-Creole core around Place des Palmistes and the Grand Marché, with pastel wooden houses, the cathedral, cafes and museums; best for first-timers who want everything walkable.
An upscale hilltop-and-coast district east of the centre with the Montabo lighthouse, ocean views and the city's grandest hotel; suits travelers wanting quiet comfort near the sea.
A leafy residential area by Bourda beach and the university, close to the market and centre; a calmer local base still near the action.
A spread-out residential suburb along the Atlantic with the city's best beaches (Rémire, Montjoly) and coastal trails up Rorota; suits families and beach-lovers with a car.
A practical residential commune between the centre and Félix Éboué airport, handy for early flights and rainforest day trips; quiet and low-key rather than scenic.

water.note: Treated and safe in central Cayenne; use bottled water in outlying areas.

transit.hours: Buses run roughly 5:30 AM to 7 PM with very limited evening and Sunday service; taxis fill the gaps after dark.
transit.note: Cayenne has no metro or tram; the Agglo'Bus network of city buses plus taxis are the main way around, and most visitors rely on a rental car for anything beyond the centre.
transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash to the driver (about €1.50-2 per ride); there is no rechargeable smartcard system.

bus: Shared taxis and minibuses to Kourou, Saint-Laurent and other towns

car.idp: Not required for EU licences; recommended otherwise

transit.m: Taxi to Cayenne centre (20-25 min; higher night, Sunday and holiday rates)
Local bus line toward Cayenne (very limited, weekday daytime only)

tip.r: Service is included by law (service compris); rounding up or leaving a euro or two for good service is appreciated but not expected.

landmarks: Place des Palmistes
Cayenne's grand central square, shaded by ranks of towering royal palms, gathers food trucks, festivals, and the statue of local statesman Félix Éboué.
Fort Cépérou
Hilltop remnants of the 17th-century fort where Cayenne was founded, overlooking tin roofs, the river estuary, and the Atlantic from the city's birthplace.
Marché de Cayenne (Central Market)
A riot of Creole, Hmong, and Brazilian flavors under one iron-framed roof, famed for its noodle soup stalls, spices, and tropical produce pyramids.
Cathédrale Saint-Sauveur
French Guiana's ochre-and-white mother church, completed in the 1930s, anchors downtown Cayenne with a graceful twin-belfry facade and cool, luminous nave.
Musée Départemental Alexandre-Franconie
In a historic Creole mansion, this museum spans stuffed jungle fauna, Amerindian artifacts, and grim relics of the penal colony era.
Plages de Rémire-Montjoly
The capital's best beaches stretch golden along the Montjoly peninsula, where giant leatherback turtles haul ashore to nest between February and July.
Hôtel de Ville de Cayenne
The elegant 19th-century city hall, built by convict labor in creamy neoclassical style, presides over palm-lined streets of colorful Creole townhouses.
Jardin Botanique de Cayenne
A shady 19th-century botanical garden of heliconias, palms, and giant water lilies offering a tranquil green pause in the equatorial heat.
Centre Spatial Guyanais (Kourou)
An hour west, Europe's equatorial spaceport launches Ariane rockets into the jungle sky; its museum and launch-pad tours thrill space enthusiasts.
Musée des Cultures Guyanaises
A regional heritage museum in an 1870s gold-miner's mansion, tracing French Guiana's Creole, Amerindian and Maroon cultures through artifacts and a reconstructed period house.

train.note: French Guiana has never had a passenger railway. The only track in the territory is the industrial line inside the Guiana Space Centre at Kourou, used to move launch vehicles; the 19th-century gold-mine and penal-colony lines were lifted long ago. Neighbouring Suriname has no passenger rail either, and the nearest working network is deep in Brazil, so everything overland here is done by road and river.

bus.note: Long-distance road transport is run by TIG (Transport Interurbain de Guyane), the Collectivite Territoriale de Guyane's nine-line network linking Cayenne with Kourou, Sinnamary, Iracoubo, Saint-Laurent-du-Maroni and Regina/Saint-Georges (https://www.ctguyane.fr/); within Cayenne the CACL runs six urban lines at about EUR 1.10 a ride. Shared taxis (taxi-co) leave the Gare Routiere when full and are faster than the scheduled buses. No coach runs straight through to another country: for Brazil take the bus to Saint-Georges de l'Oyapock, cross the Oyapock bridge to Oiapoque and pick up Brazilian services to Macapa; for Suriname go to Saint-Laurent-du-Maroni, cross the river to Albina and continue to Paramaribo. Get your exit stamp at the PAF border post before crossing - it is not automatic.

intl.to: Albina (Suriname) - vehicle and passenger bac across the Maroni from Saint-Laurent-du-Maroni, ~3 hr west of Cayenne
Oiapoque (Brazil) - river pirogues from Saint-Georges de l'Oyapock, ~3.5 hr southeast of Cayenne; a road bridge is also open
intl.op: local pirogue operators, pay at the landing

intl.to: Iles du Salut / Devil's Island (French Guiana) - catamaran from Kourou, ~1 hr from Cayenne
intl.op: Kourou excursion-boat operators, book through the Kourou tourist office

ferry.note: Cayenne itself has no passenger terminal - the territory's commercial port is Degrad des Cannes, a cargo harbour a few kilometres downriver handling around 700,000 tonnes a year and no scheduled sailings. The boats that matter are the border crossings: the official bac carries cars and foot passengers across the Maroni between Saint-Laurent-du-Maroni and Albina several times a day, supplemented by faster informal pirogues that do not deal with immigration for you. The Oyapock crossing to Brazil can now also be made by road bridge, open since 2017, though the pirogues still run. The other regular boat is the hour-long catamaran from Kourou out to the Iles du Salut, weather- and tide-dependent and worth booking a day or two ahead in high season.

full.name: Îles du Salut
